original_position: Surviving findings (severity-ordered): (1) polymorphic/tenant-variable QUERYABLE schema = high/MEDIUM; (2) aggregate-centric bounded-document read/write = high/MEDIUM, with caveat that cross-aggregate queries and 16MiB-limit growth narrow MongoDB's edge; (3) non-additive DDL on hot tables = medium/MEDIUM, downgraded from peers' critical because at MVP table sizes rewrites are sub-second, lock_timeout neutralizes the cascade, and PostgreSQL 18 NOT NULL NOT VALID removes the SET NOT NULL scan; (4) write-heavy partial updates on large JSONB = medium/LOW. Refuted: prior-MongoDB-codebase (symmetric, not Postgres-specific), 60-day operational bloat (below MVP autovacuum thresholds), connection exhaustion (solved by managed-service built-in pooling). Acceptability: keep Postgres if core entities have stable schemas, access is relational not aggregate-scoped, tenant variance is non-queryable blobs, and a managed PG18 service with pooling is used; else run a 2-day spike.

Three conditions where Postgres is strictly worse: (1) core persisted objects still change in NON-ADDITIVE ways after production traffic (type changes, later NOT NULL, validated constraints, volatile defaults on hot tables) = critical/HIGH; explicitly narrows it — additive evolution and future-only default changes are NOT the failure mode; (2) dominant unit of work is a bounded nested aggregate fetched/updated whole, few cross-aggregate joins = high/HIGH; (3) heterogeneity is a first-class MVP requirement (tenant-defined fields, queryable integration payloads, per-customer variant field sets) = medium/HIGH. Acceptable only if production schema changes are mostly additive, the hot path is not a bounded document aggregate, and tenant/integration variability is peripheral rather than first-class queryable.

Six surviving findings ranked: (1) polymorphic/tenant-variable queryable schema = HIGH/MEDIUM; (2) aggregate-scoped read/write = HIGH/MEDIUM; (3) non-additive schema churn on hot tables = MEDIUM/MEDIUM (additive changes are near-free, so fires only when >30% of changes are non-additive); (4) serverless/FaaS deployment connection model = MEDIUM/MEDIUM (conditional, not stated in problem); (5) large-JSONB write-heavy = MEDIUM/LOW (benchmark evidence is configuration-asymmetric and unreliable); (6) self-managed infra without Postgres expertise = LOW/MEDIUM (evaporates with a managed service). Acceptable if at least four of six conditions hold; if three or more fail, or finding 1 or 2 applies at full strength, a 2-day spike against the actual top-10 queries is required; absent that the choice is underdetermined rather than Postgres-wrong.

Four findings: (1) serverless/FaaS connection exhaustion against default max_connections=100 = critical/HIGH; (2) non-additive DDL (type changes, NOT NULL on populated columns) triggering ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock cascades = high/HIGH; (3) frequent partial updates to large embedded documents incurring MVCC full-row + GIN rewrite bloat = high/MEDIUM; (4) prior-codebase/sunk-cost argument = low/LOW (conceded as symmetric). Acceptable only when the core domain admits a stable ER diagram for the top five entities before month one, deployment is a single long-lived process, at least one engineer owns vacuum and connection-pool monitoring, and primary access patterns are relational joins rather than partial document mutation. (Note: in earlier rounds this worker leaned toward 'no qualifying condition exists within the 6-month constraint,' which peers contradicted.)
